sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Caesar opens his Commentaries with the Helvetii, a people hemmed in by the Rhine, the Jura and the Lake of Geneva. Their noble Orgetorix persuaded them to leave their land in full force; when his bid for kingship was exposed he died before he could be tried, but the Helvetii went ahead. In 58 BCE they burned their towns, villages and spare corn and set out, with neighbouring peoples and the Boii, to settle in the west near the Santones. The easy road ran through the Roman Province by the bridge at Geneva. Caesar, newly in command of the Gallic provinces, hurried from Rome, broke the bridge and closed the Rhone crossings.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Caesar presents the campaign as the defence of the Province. He recalls that within living memory the Helvetii had killed the consul Lucius Cassius and sent his army under the yoke, and argues that a warlike people near Tolosa would endanger a rich and unprotected district. Dio is less generous: Caesar's wish to be at war for the whole of his command was being granted, and he chose to drive the Helvetii back with Gallic help, fearing for Tolosa, before the tribes could come to terms with each other. The appeals of the Aedui, the Ambarri and the Allobroges, whose lands the migrants were plundering, gave him allies and a cause beyond the Province.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Caesar's first object was to keep the Helvetii out of the Province, and his second, once they were in the lands of Rome's allies, to stop the migration. The Helvetii wanted new land. After the defeat at the Saône their envoy Divico offered to settle wherever Caesar chose if he made peace; Caesar demanded hostages and satisfaction for the Aedui and the Allobroges, and Divico answered that the Helvetii were used to receiving hostages, not giving them.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The migrants turned from the Rhone narrows through the land of the Sequani and the Aedui, crossed the Saône (the Arar), whose current Caesar calls beyond belief for slowness, and moved north. The battle takes its name from Bibracte, by Caesar's account the largest and best-provided town of the Aedui, toward which he had turned for corn and from which he was then less than a day's march. The 1911 Britannica places Bibracte on Mont Beuvray near Autun, where excavation had found a rampart, houses, a temple and metalworkers' shops; the museum at the foot of the mountain presents it as the Aeduan capital. The battle was fought on hills some distance from the town; the Loeb edition's map follows Colonel Stoffel, who found an entrenchment on the ground, and Colonel Bircher's placing of the troops.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Caesar commanded veteran legions, two newly raised in Nearer Gaul and cavalry levied in the Province and among the Aedui and their allies. Titus Labienus, his lieutenant, held the Rhone works and later led the flanking force before the battle. The Helvetii marched as a people, with families and carts; the Boii and Tulingi formed their rearguard, and Divico, who had commanded against Cassius, spoke for them. Inside Caesar's camp the Aeduan Dumnorix, brother of the loyal Diviciacus, was obstructing the corn supply and informing the enemy, according to the Aeduan magistrate Liscus. Caesar's figures for the migrants, which he says came from registers found in their camp, are not repeated.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: When the Helvetii turned to pursue him, Caesar withdrew to the nearest hill and sent his horse to delay them. He drew up the veteran legions in three lines halfway up the slope and posted the new legions and the auxiliaries on the summit, where the packs were gathered and entrenched. The Helvetii parked their carts in one place, threw back the Roman horse and came up the hill in a close mass. Dio describes the same sequence: the cavalry sent forward to buy time while Caesar formed on higher ground.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Caesar fell on the canton still on the near bank of the Saône, bridged the river in a day and followed the main body. For about a fortnight the armies marched close together; after a cavalry reverse Caesar refused battle and was content to stop the migrants plundering. A planned dawn attack failed when Publius Considius, sent ahead with the scouts, reported that the height Labienus had been sent to seize was held by the enemy, when Labienus held it. Next day, with the corn ration due, Caesar turned for Bibracte and the Helvetii followed. The battle began after midday: a javelin volley broke the Helvetian mass, which fell back to a height; the Boii and Tulingi struck the Roman flank, and the third line turned to meet them. The fighting around the wagon laager went on far into the night. Plutarch adds that women and children died defending the wagons.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Caesar bought time on the Rhone by asking the Helvetian envoys to come back on a fixed day and used it to build his entrenchment, then refused them passage; Dio says he held out hope of agreement while he made the road impassable. At the Saône he struck the part of the migration that had not crossed. After the cavalry reverse he followed without fighting. When the corn ran short he broke away toward Bibracte, which the Helvetii read as retreat. Attacked, he had his own horse and then every officer's sent out of sight, as he explains, to make the danger equal and remove hope of flight. Plutarch turns this into a saying: the horse would serve for the pursuit after victory.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: When the Boii and Tulingi came onto the Roman flank and the beaten Helvetii turned back from their height, Caesar's third line faced about while the first two held the front, so the two-sided fight did not become an envelopment. The storm of the wagon laager at night ended the migrants' resistance, and lack of every provision brought their envoys to Caesar a few days later.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The survivors marched night and day to the Lingones, whom Caesar forbade to help them. When the Helvetii surrendered he demanded hostages, arms and runaway slaves. A canton that slipped away toward the Rhine by night was brought back, and in Caesar's words treated as enemies. The rest were ordered home to rebuild the towns they had burned, with corn from the Allobroges, and the Aedui were allowed to settle the Boii among themselves.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Caesar gives his reason for sending the Helvetii home: he did not want their good land left empty for Germans from across the Rhine to occupy, beside the Province. Plutarch and the 1911 Britannica give the same reason. The Britannica continues that the Gallic chiefs then appealed to Caesar against the German king Ariovistus, whom he defeated that same year. The pattern of the Gallic command was set: an intervention on behalf of allies that ended in Roman control of their country.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An army that pursues beyond its supply hands the initiative to the pursued: Caesar's turn toward Bibracte, forced by the corn ration and the Aedui's delays, brought on the battle he had failed to force. A line formed on a slope before the attack arrives can absorb a surprise on the march. And a migration is not only an army: the families at the wagons were where the fighting lasted longest.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Caesar's narrative is the only full account, written by the commander for readers in Rome. Its figures for the migration, which he says were drawn from registers in Greek letters found in the Helvetian camp, are not used; Plutarch's differ. Plutarch credits the destruction of the Tigurini at the Saône to Labienus, where Caesar says he led the attack himself. Dio has Orgetorix lead the migration, where Caesar says he died before it began. Dio also makes Caesar deceive the envoys with hope; Caesar says only that he took time to consider. Caesar's phrase for the fate of the runaways leaves what happened to them unstated. The exact battlefield is a modern reconstruction.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Caesar's Gallic War 1, in H. J. Edwards's Loeb translation on LacusCurtius, is the main narrative. Plutarch's Life of Caesar and Cassius Dio's Book 38, also in Loeb translations on LacusCurtius, are later Greek retellings that differ on the Saône and on Caesar's dealings with the envoys. The 1911 Britannica's articles on the Helvetii, on Bibracte and on Caesar give a modern frame, and the website of Bibracte presents the Aeduan town on Mount Beuvray and its museum.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the campaigns of 58 against the Helvetii and Ariovistus, the Belgae of north-western Gaul formed a league against Rome; only the Remi stayed friendly and warned Caesar. In the spring of 57 he marched north, checked the Belgic army at the Aisne and watched it break up as it went home, short of food and alarmed by an Aeduan invasion of its lands. The Nervii, with the Atrebates and the Viromandui, stayed in arms. After three days' march through the land of the Ambiani, prisoners told Caesar that they were waiting beyond the river Sabis, that the Atuatuci were on the way, and that their families had been sent into the marshes.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The 1911 Britannica says Caesar marched to anticipate a Belgic offensive he understood to be in preparation; Dio says the Belgae, seeing his success, feared that he would come for them next. Either way the war of 57 carried the Gallic command from the defence of the Province, its claim in 58, into the conquest of northern Gaul. Caesar ends his account with praise of the Nervii's courage, which also magnified his victory for readers in Rome.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Caesar meant to bring the Nervii to battle and end resistance in the north. The Nervii meant to destroy his army piece by piece: Belgic informers who had marched with the Romans told them that each legion was separated by a long baggage train, so the first legion could be attacked at the camp while the rest were far behind. The sight of the baggage was to be their signal.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Caesar's camp was marked out on a hill sloping evenly down to the river. Opposite rose a matching slope, open near the water and so thickly wooded higher up that the enemy could hide in it; the river was about three feet deep. The Nervii, who had almost no cavalry, grew hedges of bent saplings and brambles against raiding horsemen, and these blocked the view across the field. The plan in the Loeb edition, after Colonel Stoffel, and the 1911 Britannica put the battle on the Sambre; the Livius article holds, citing Pierre Turquin's study of 1955, that it was the Selle, and places the Roman slope west of Saulzoir.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Caesar marched with his legions, cavalry, slingers, archers and Numidians, the two newest legions guarding the baggage; Labienus and the legates commanded under him. Treveran horsemen served as auxiliaries. The Nervii relied on infantry and fought under Boduognatus, their commander-in-chief, with the Atrebates and the Viromandui beside them; the Atuatuci had not yet arrived. The figures the Nervian envoys later gave are not repeated.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Because he was approaching the enemy, Caesar followed his usual practice and changed the order of march: the legions in light order went first, the baggage of the whole army behind them, and the two recently raised legions at the rear. The cavalry, slingers and archers crossed the river and skirmished with the enemy's horse, which kept withdrawing into the wood. The leading legions marked out the camp and set to work.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: When the head of the baggage train came in sight, the Nervii broke from the wood, scattered the cavalry and crossed the river so fast that they seemed at the wood's edge, in the river and on the Romans at once. With no time to form, the soldiers fell in wherever they stood. On the left the Ninth and Tenth drove the Atrebates into the river and pursued them across it; in the centre the Eleventh and Eighth broke the Viromandui and fought on the banks. That left the front of the camp and the Twelfth and Seventh on the right exposed, and the Nervii, in a dense column under Boduognatus, enveloped the right and entered the camp. Cavalry, sutlers and the Treveri fled. Caesar went to the right, then had the two legions there close together. The rear legions appeared on the crest, and Labienus, who had taken the Nervian camp, sent the Tenth back. The Nervii fought on from the heaps of their dead until they were cut down.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: By Caesar's account two orders given before the attack saved the army: the changed order of march, and the instruction that every legate stay with his legion until the camp was fortified, so that the legates acted without waiting for him. In the crisis he took a shield from a soldier in the rear, went into the front line, called on the centurions by name and ordered the ranks opened so the men could use their swords; he then told the tribunes to join the two hard-pressed legions so that they could face in any direction. He says he gave only the essential orders and that there was time for few of the rest.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The return of the Tenth from the captured Nervian camp, sent by Labienus when he saw the Roman camp from the higher ground, and the arrival of the rear legions on the crest turned a half-lost camp into a victory. Caesar writes that even the wounded fought again, propped on their shields, and the sutlers attacked the enemy unarmed.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Nervii were all but destroyed as a fighting people. Their elders in the marshes surrendered, and Caesar, wishing to be seen to show mercy to suppliants, left them their land and towns and ordered their neighbours not to harm them.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The campaign went on against the Atuatuci, who submitted and were later sold into slavery for what the 1911 Britannica calls treachery, while Caesar's lieutenant Publius Crassus received the submission of other peoples; by the Britannica's account almost all Gaul except Aquitania acknowledged Roman supremacy by the year's end. The battle also fixed a picture of the army and its general: Plutarch makes Caesar's daring the reason his men fought beyond their strength.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Trained troops can act without orders when there is no time to give them; Caesar credits his soldiers' experience and his standing order to the legates. Reconnaissance was the weak point: informers in his own column betrayed his routine, and the cavalry screen could not see into the wood. A victorious wing that pursues across a river leaves the centre and the camp open.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Caesar's is the only detailed narrative, and the Livius article notes that he almost admits he was caught off guard. Plutarch has the Seventh and Twelfth surrounded and all their centurions killed, and says the Tenth ran down from the heights when it saw Caesar in danger. Dio, in a passage with a gap in the text, tells a different battle: the Nervii fled where Caesar was, while the larger part took his camp, and he turned back from the pursuit to surround them at their plunder. Lendering points out that the losses the Nervian envoys reported conflict with Caesar's own figures elsewhere and calls them an exaggeration; they are not repeated here. The river is disputed between the Sambre and the Selle.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Caesar's Gallic War 2, in H. J. Edwards's Loeb translation on LacusCurtius, is the main narrative. The Livius article by Jona Lendering quotes Anne and Peter Wiseman's translation of the battle chapters and adds his own judgements and photographs of the Selle. Plutarch's Life of Caesar and Cassius Dio's Book 39, in Loeb translations on LacusCurtius, are later versions that differ from Caesar and from each other. The 1911 Britannica's article on Caesar sets the battle in the campaign of 57.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Roman expansion had brought Rome to the Parthian frontier: Lucullus and Pompey pressed on Parthian dependencies, and Gabinius backed a rebel against the Parthian king Orodes II. Shahbazi argues that the war followed from a century of converging expansion rather than simply from Crassus's ambition.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Crassus, one of the triumvirs, received Syria as his province in 55 BCE. Plutarch says he boasted of conquests as far as Bactria and India, and that Caesar encouraged the war and sent Gallic cavalry under Crassus's son Publius. Shahbazi notes that Crassus plundered temples at Jerusalem and Hierapolis during his first year in Syria.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Crassus aimed to strike toward Seleucia and Ctesiphon. King Artavasdes II of Armenia urged a route through the Armenian hills, where Parthian cavalry would be least effective; Crassus chose Mesopotamia, where he had garrisons. Orodes then invaded Armenia himself, while Surena waited in Mesopotamia with his own horsemen.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought on the plain near Carrhae (Harran), close to the river Balikh. Plutarch describes deep sand and a waterless waste, but Livius describes a steppe with rivers and farmland, and Shahbazi doubts that the route lacked water in spring.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Crassus led legions with cavalry and light infantry, together with Arab and Osrhoenian allies. Surena commanded his own levies: mailed cavalry and horse archers with a powerful compound bow, backed by a camel train loaded with arrows. Shahbazi notes that the Romans had no experience of such archery and, on foot, could neither escape nor catch the horsemen.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Crassus formed a hollow square with cavalry along its sides; Shahbazi, following modern reconstructions, places Cassius on the left by the river, Crassus in the centre and Publius on the right. The Parthians approached unseen behind rising ground and kept their armour covered until they were close.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Shahbazi dates the battle to the afternoon of 6 May 53 BCE, 9 June in the Roman calendar of the time. The Romans reached the Balikh tired, and Crassus pressed on rather than camp. The Parthians surrounded the square and kept shooting, their arrows resupplied from the camels. Publius led a sortie, was drawn away by a feigned retreat, surrounded and killed; the Parthians returned with his head on a lance and shot at the square until nightfall.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Crassus's choices of the Mesopotamian route, of pressing on past the Balikh without rest and of sending Publius out became the familiar charges against him. Surena's decision to bring a camel train of arrows meant that his archers did not run out; Livius judges that this settled the battle.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The destruction of Publius's force cost Crassus his cavalry and his only offensive option. His Osrhoenian and Arab allies had already left the field, which Roman writers later called treachery.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: That night the legates led the army away to Carrhae, leaving the wounded, whom the Parthians killed or took prisoner. A further night march toward the Armenian hills failed for Crassus's own group. Surena offered a parley; a scuffle broke out, and Crassus and his officers were killed. His head and hand were sent to Orodes.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Shahbazi says the victory halted Roman expansion, returned Mesopotamia to Parthia and fixed the Euphrates as the boundary, beginning centuries of rivalry. Crassus's death left Pompey and Caesar as the remaining triumvirs. Captured Romans were settled at Merv, and Orodes later had Surena executed. The lost standards came back only through a peace negotiated by Tiberius in 20 BCE.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Missile fire decides a battle only if it can be sustained: Surena's supply train turned archery into fire that an infantry army could not answer. An army without effective missile troops and cavalry of its own could not close with a mobile enemy, and choosing a route meant choosing terrain and allies.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The traditional story blames Crassus's greed, a treacherous guide and a waterless desert. Shahbazi argues that the duplicity of Abgar of Osrhoene, Plutarch's Ariamnes, cannot be demonstrated, and Livius treats treachery and the desert as later excuses. Plutarch's narrative is a moral tale full of omens, though Shahbazi thinks it draws on a well-informed eyewitness. Plutarch's army sizes and losses, including his seven legions, are not repeated as fact, and the sources place the battlefield variously south and east of Carrhae.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Plutarch's Life of Crassus is the main narrative. Shahbazi's Encyclopaedia Iranica entry, read in a browser, evaluates it alongside Dio Cassius, whose account was not read here. Livius gives a shorter assessment of the supply and terrain arguments and the later course of the wars.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Early in 52 BCE Roman traders were massacred at Cenabum and the Arverni rose under Vercingetorix. Caesar took Avaricum, whose occupants were massacred, and then divided his army: Labienus went north against the Senones and the Parisii, and Caesar marched up the Allier toward Gergovia, the Arvernian capital. Vercingetorix broke the bridges and shadowed him along the far bank, but Caesar hid part of his force, rebuilt a bridge on its old piles while the rest marched on, and crossed. Dio tells the crossing differently, by rafts built while the Gauls watched the column ahead.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Aedui, Rome's oldest allies in Gaul, were wavering. Convictolitavis, whom Caesar had confirmed as their chief magistrate, took an Arvernian bribe and persuaded young nobles led by Litaviccus that the Aedui alone stood between Gaul and victory. Litaviccus turned the Aeduan force marching to join Caesar with an invented story that the Romans had killed the Aeduan horsemen and their chiefs, and Romans travelling with it were tortured and killed. Caesar's narrative makes the siege a race between his army and the defection of his allies; Dio links the defeat to the same cause, saying the Romans were beaten while Caesar was away dealing with the Aedui.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Caesar judged the town too strong to storm and would not blockade it until his corn supply was secure. He took a hill opposite the town to cut the defenders off from much of their water and forage. After the Aeduan crisis his aim changed: by his own account he was planning how to leave Gergovia and reunite his army without making the departure look like flight, and he describes the assault as a bid for surprise, not a battle. Vercingetorix's aim was to hold the heights and refuse battle on level ground.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Gergovia stood on a very high hill with difficult approaches on every side; Vercingetorix camped the contingent of each state separately on the ridge, holding every point with a view. Caesar's large camp lay below, joined by a double ditch to a lesser camp on the captured hill. Halfway up the slope the Gauls had built a stone wall, and above it their camps filled the hillside to the town wall; a valley separated part of the assaulting force from the rest. Dio stresses that the Romans, camped in the plain, were overlooked and could not reach the heights with their missiles. The 1911 Britannica places Gergovia on a hill about eight miles from the Puy de Dôme. The plateau that Napoleon III's excavations identified, and that was renamed Gergovie in 1865, carries the monument and the museum; an association founded with Paul Eychart's support argues instead for the Côtes de Clermont, north of Clermont-Ferrand.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Caesar commanded with a legate at the head of each legion. Gaius Fabius held the camps while Caesar marched against the Aeduan column, and Titus Sextius the lesser camp during the assault. The Aedui supplied cavalry and an infantry force, until Litaviccus turned it; the Aeduan nobles Eporedorix and Viridomarus served with Caesar. Vercingetorix led a coalition: he met the chiefs of the states in council every dawn and tested his men daily in cavalry skirmishes with archers among the horsemen. Teutomatus, king of the Nitiobriges, was among his allies.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: For the assault Caesar drew the enemy to the far side of the town. Cavalry ranged noisily round the hills at night; at dawn muleteers in helmets rode round like cavalry, and a legion was shown and then hidden in the woods. While the Gauls hurried to fortify the threatened hill, he moved soldiers in small parties into the lesser camp with their badges covered, told his legates to keep the men in hand, warned them of the ground, and sent the Aedui up by another ascent on the right.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: After crossing the Allier, Caesar reached Gergovia in five days, reconnoitred and took the hill opposite by night. When the Aeduan column was turned, he marched out with most of his army, recovered it without bloodshed and came back by forced march to relieve Fabius, whose camp had been attacked all day. Then came the assault. At the signal the legions crossed the stone wall and took three camps, so suddenly that King Teutomatus escaped half-dressed. Caesar sounded the retreat and halted the Tenth, but the other legions, beyond the valley, did not hear and went on to the walls. Women on the walls first begged for mercy, then, as Gallic reinforcements arrived, urged their own men on. The Aedui, appearing on the Roman flank in arms like the enemy's, caused alarm; the attackers were driven down, and the Tenth and cohorts of the Thirteenth checked the pursuit.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Caesar chose not to storm or blockade at once, but to seize the hill that threatened the enemy's water. When the Aedui were turned, he left the siege with most of his army and forbade his men to kill any of the column, and the Aedui returned to their allegiance. The assault was a limited surprise meant to cover a withdrawal, with Sextius's cohorts posted at the foot of the hill and Caesar himself advancing with the Tenth in case of a repulse. After the defeat he offered battle on level ground for two days; when Vercingetorix declined, he marched into Aeduan territory and recrossed the Allier.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The recall failed. The legions beyond the valley did not hear the trumpet and, in Caesar's account, pressed on against the efforts of their tribunes and legates, carried away by hope and earlier success. The Gauls from the far side of the town returned in force, and the sight of the Aedui on the flank turned an advance into a rout.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The assault failed with heavy loss among the centurions, and Caesar raised the siege. Dio says he had been repulsed throughout, lost a number of soldiers and saw that the town could not be taken. The defeat emboldened the Aedui to revolt; Litaviccus went to rouse their state, and Eporedorix and Viridomarus asked to go ahead of him; Caesar, though he expected the revolt, let them go.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Within weeks, by the 1911 Britannica's account, Caesar had marched toward the Province, beaten Vercingetorix near Dijon and shut him in Alesia. Suetonius counts the rout of a legion at Gergovia among only three reverses in Caesar's Gallic wars. Caesar himself later used it as an example: after his defeat at Dyrrhachium he told his army that the loss might be turned to advantage, as it had been at Gergovia.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A deception can work and the plan still fail if its limits cannot be enforced: the surprise succeeded, but the halt depended on a signal half the army could not hear. Caesar's speech the next day states the problem as he saw it: he required discipline and self-restraint no less than courage. A siege by an army whose allies are wavering places the commander in two places at once.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Caesar is the only full source. He explains the defeat by his soldiers' disobedience and the unfavourable ground, and insists that the plan was a surprise, not a battle, a reading that protects his judgement. Dio describes a long, failing siege and ties the defeat to Caesar's absence among the Aedui. The losses Caesar gives are not repeated here. The site itself is disputed: the association's history of the controversy traces the identification of the plateau of Merdogne to a sixteenth-century scholar, Gabriele Simeoni, and to Colonel Stoffel's excavations for Napoleon III, and the rival case for the Côtes de Clermont to Maurice Busset in 1933 and Paul Eychart from 1952. That account comes from one side of the debate.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Caesar's Gallic War 7.34–54, in H. J. Edwards's Loeb translation on LacusCurtius, is the main narrative, and the Civil War 3.73 shows how he recalled the defeat later. Cassius Dio's Book 40 and Suetonius's Life of Julius Caesar, also in Loeb translations there, give a later Greek narrative and a Roman biographer's verdict. The 1911 Britannica's articles on Gergovia and on Caesar give a modern outline, and the website of the ASCOT association sets out the controversy over the site from the point of view of those who reject the official one.

phases.title: Crossing the Allier
phases.description: Vercingetorix breaks the bridges; Caesar hides part of his army and rebuilds one on its old piles.

phases.title: Before the town
phases.description: Caesar reconnoitres, waits for corn and takes the hill opposite the town by night.

phases.title: The Aeduan crisis
phases.description: Litaviccus turns the Aeduan column; Caesar recovers it by a night march while Fabius holds the camps.

phases.title: The assault
phases.description: A feint draws the Gauls away; the legions take three camps, miss the recall and are driven down from the walls.

phases.title: Withdrawal
phases.description: Caesar reprimands the army, offers battle on level ground for two days and marches to the Allier.

perspectives.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
perspectives.objective: Take or isolate the Arvernian capital and then, as the Aedui wavered, withdraw without appearing beaten.
perspectives.known: The town was too strong to storm; deserters said the Gauls feared for the wooded hill on the far side.
perspectives.uncertainty: The loyalty of the Aedui and of the troops they had sent him.
perspectives.constraints: His corn supply, a camp too large for a small garrison, and an uphill attack over broken ground.
perspectives.forces: Legions under their legates, with Aeduan allies of doubtful loyalty.
perspectives.terrain: A high plateau whose every approach was overlooked, and a valley dividing his assaulting legions.
perspectives.logistics: He would not begin a blockade until his corn was secured, and the Aeduan crisis made supply uncertain.
perspectives.decision: He attempted a limited surprise attack, with reserves posted to cover a repulse.
perspectives.outcome: The legions went beyond the recall and were driven back, and he raised the siege.

perspectives.name: Vercingetorix
perspectives.objective: Hold Gergovia and the heights around it and refuse battle on level ground.
perspectives.known: The Romans had taken the hill opposite and could cut off water and forage; the wooded hill on the far side was the town's weak point.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where Caesar would strike, under movements he could watch but not read.
perspectives.constraints: A coalition of separate contingents held together by daily councils.
perspectives.forces: Contingents of many states camped apart, and cavalry with archers among them.
perspectives.terrain: The plateau and its heights, with a stone wall built halfway up the slope.
perspectives.logistics: Water and forage from the land round the town, threatened by the Roman works.
perspectives.decision: He moved his men to fortify the threatened hill, then brought them back in force when the town was attacked.
perspectives.outcome: His men drove the Romans down; he declined battle on the plain and let Caesar go.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 52 BCE Vercingetorix's forces occupied Alesia during the resistance to Caesar's conquest of Gaul.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Caesar's account presents Roman command from the conqueror's perspective. Political self-presentation shapes the narrative. Plutarch sets the revolt in its wider frame: led by the Arverni and Carnutes, it chose Vercingetorix as supreme commander, and Plutarch judges that had it come a little later, when Caesar was caught up in the civil war, Italy would have faced a terror like the Cimbri; the defection of the Aedui, long called brothers of the Romans, dismayed Caesar's army.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Romans sought surrender by siege; the defenders awaited a relief army.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Caesar describes a hilltop settlement, nearby rivers, a plain and surrounding heights. The museum interprets the site at Alise-Sainte-Reine.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Caesar directed Roman legions and cavalry; Vercingetorix led the besieged force. Several Gallic leaders shared command of the relief army.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Roman works faced both the settlement and the approaching relief force.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Investment was followed by relief attempts, attacks from inside and outside, and the defeat of the relieving army. Cassius Dio adds a grim episode: as food ran short, Vercingetorix drove out the children, the women and those least useful, hoping the Romans would take them as booty; Caesar, short of food himself and expecting them to be taken back, forced them back, and they perished between the town and the Roman camp because neither side would receive them. Dio also describes the hidden pits and stakes that broke the relief army's night attack on the outer lines.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Caesar reports moving reserves to threatened sectors and sending cavalry around the outer works.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: In his narrative, Roman reinforcement and a cavalry attack in the rear broke the final external assault.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Vercingetorix surrendered. Caesar distributed many prisoners as enslaved captives. The later writers dramatise the surrender differently: Plutarch has Vercingetorix ride out in his finest armour on a decorated horse, circle Caesar, then dismount, strip off his armour and sit silent at his feet; Dio has him come unannounced, hoping for pardon on the strength of a former friendship, and kneel in supplication, while Caesar reproached him with that very friendship, put him in chains and later had him executed after the triumph.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The result strengthened Roman domination while imposing conquest and captivity on the defeated population.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Study siege engineering together with food supply and coordination. Static fortifications still required decisions about mobile reserves.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Enemy numbers and dramatic speeches come from Caesar's interested account. The displayed phases simplify an extended siege, not a measured hour-by-hour reconstruction. Plutarch preserves a trace of the Gallic memory of the war: the Arverni showed a short sword hanging in a temple which they said had been taken from Caesar, who, seeing it later, smiled and would not let it be taken down. The surrender scene differs between Plutarch and Dio, and Dio's account of the noncombatants expelled from the town has no counterpart in Plutarch. Both later authors show how the story was retold, and neither is an eyewitness; Plutarch's figures are not used. No Gallic narrative survives.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Caesar supplies the principal narrative; museum archaeology and landscape interpretation provide a different kind of evidence. Plutarch's Life of Caesar and Cassius Dio's Roman History 40, both in the Loeb translations on LacusCurtius, give later Greek retellings that differ from Caesar on the surrender and the fate of the noncombatants.

phases.title: Investment
phases.description: Roman works close around Alesia.

phases.title: Double front
phases.description: The Romans prepare to defend against forces outside and inside.

phases.title: Relief assaults
phases.description: The relief army attacks while the besieged attempt sorties.

phases.title: Surrender
phases.description: Vercingetorix is surrendered and the defenders lose their freedom.

perspectives.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
perspectives.objective: Force the surrender of Vercingetorix's army before a Gallic relief force could break the siege.
perspectives.known: Vercingetorix had sent his cavalry out to summon a relief army from across Gaul.
perspectives.uncertainty: When the relief force would arrive and where it would attack.
perspectives.constraints: Food and fodder for his legions, and long lines to man against two fronts at once.
perspectives.forces: Roman legions with allied cavalry, including Germanic horsemen.
perspectives.terrain: The hilltop settlement, its rivers and the surrounding heights set the course of the works. A weak point on the outer line became the focus of the final assault.
perspectives.logistics: He gathered supplies to sustain the army inside its lines.
perspectives.decision: He built inner and outer lines and, in the final assaults, moved reserves to threatened sectors and sent cavalry outside the works. The record of these decisions is Caesar's own.
perspectives.outcome: Vercingetorix surrendered. Caesar's narrative presents the victory as his personal achievement.

perspectives.name: Vercingetorix and the Gallic relief commanders
perspectives.objective: Hold Alesia until a relief army could break the Roman lines from outside.
perspectives.known: Food in the settlement was limited, and a relief army was being raised across Gaul.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the relief army would arrive before supplies ran out.
perspectives.constraints: Coordinating attacks from inside and outside the Roman lines without reliable communication.
perspectives.forces: The besieged army in the settlement and a relief army under several commanders, including Vercassivellaunus.
perspectives.terrain: Roman works blocked access across the plain and the surrounding hills.
perspectives.logistics: Caesar reports that the Mandubii, inhabitants of Alesia, were expelled to save food and were refused passage through the Roman lines; Dio says Vercingetorix drove out the women, children and others least useful, who died between the lines.
perspectives.decision: Breakouts were timed with the relief army's assaults. After those failed, Vercingetorix surrendered. Gallic decisions are known almost entirely through Caesar.
perspectives.outcome: Surrender, captivity and enslavement for many of the defeated; Dio says Vercingetorix, who had hoped for pardon, was executed after Caesar's triumph.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Early in 49 BCE Caesar drove Pompey out of Italy, but Pompey's legates held Spain with veteran legions: Afranius the nearer province, Petreius Lusitania and Varro the further province. Caesar sent Gaius Fabius ahead to seize the Pyrenean passes and followed; the 1911 Britannica dates his arrival at Ilerda to 23 June. Afranius and Petreius had joined forces there because of the natural strength of the position, while Varro held the south.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Plutarch says Caesar meant to leave no enemy in his rear before marching against Pompey. Opinion in Rome counted: when Afranius and Petreius sent home exaggerated reports of Caesar's troubles, crowds congratulated Afranius's household and men set out from Italy to join Pompey, and Dio says Romans at home gave Caesar up for lost. Before the campaign Caesar borrowed money from his tribunes and centurions and gave it to the soldiers, which, he writes, bound the officers to him by the debt and the men by the bounty. His account, written for the same public, stresses his reluctance to shed citizens' blood.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Afranius and Petreius meant to hold Ilerda and its bridge and, when that became unsafe, to carry the war into Celtiberia, where Pompey's name was strong and Caesar's barely known, and to prolong it into the winter. Caesar's aim, as he states it, was to cut them off from food and water and finish the business without exposing his men to battle.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Ilerda stood on a hill by the river Sicoris, with the Pompeian camp on the next height and a narrow plain between them, a mound in its middle. Caesar's camp lay between the Sicoris and the Cinga, which a flood could make impassable. To the south lay the Ebro, the town of Octogesa and a belt of rugged hills and defiles that whoever reached first could hold against the other. Dio calls the region bowl-shaped and terribly dry.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Afranius and Petreius shared command of Pompey's legions in Spain, with heavy and light auxiliaries from both provinces and cavalry. Caesar had veteran legions, cavalry from Gaul and lightly armed Germans. He describes the Afranian infantry as fighting in loose order, charging and giving ground without shame, a style learned against the Lusitanians. The two Pompeian commanders decided by council and disagreed; on Caesar's side, officers and men pressed him openly to fight. No figures are given here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Caesar arrived to find that a storm had broken one of Fabius's two bridges over the Sicoris and that Plancus had held off Afranius until relieved. He offered battle in three lines below the Pompeian camp; Afranius stayed on the slope. Caesar then entrenched close by, digging a ditch with the front lines standing under arms rather than raising a rampart the enemy could see.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: First came the fight for the mound, lost to the faster Afranians, and a struggle of five hours under the walls of the town. Then a flood broke both of Caesar's bridges, cutting him off from his allies and his convoys while the Pompeians had plenty. Caesar built light boats of a kind he had seen in Britain, carried them overland, crossed upstream and bridged the river, and communities began to come over to him. Afranius and Petreius set out for the Ebro; Caesar's infantry forded the Sicoris, which he had partly diverted, caught the column and, marching by no road, reached the defiles first. Cut off from the Ebro and then from water, the Pompeians tried to return to Ilerda under constant attack, killed their baggage animals and asked for terms. The 1911 Britannica dates the submission to 2 August.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Caesar's choices were to restore his communications by building boats rather than wait for the water to fall; to divert part of the Sicoris to make a ford; to let the army attempt the ford when the men demanded it, after setting the weakest aside; to march across country by no marked road to get ahead of the enemy; and, above all, to refuse battle when his legates, centurions and tribunes demanded it against a shaken enemy. He writes that he hoped to win by cutting off supply, asked why he should lose soldiers even in a successful battle, and was moved by compassion for fellow citizens.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The bridge upstream reversed the supply situation within days, and the arrival at the defiles ahead of the Pompeian column closed the road to the Ebro. The soldiers of the two armies then began to visit each other's camps and talk of surrender; Petreius broke up the talks, had Caesarians found in his camp killed and made his army swear a new oath, while Caesar sent the Pompeians in his camp back unharmed. That delayed the end by a few days.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Afranius asked for terms in the hearing of both armies. Caesar answered that he wanted only the armies raised against him disbanded: men with homes in Spain were released at once and the rest at the river Varus, none was to be forced to swear allegiance to him, and he fed them on the march and paid for property his soldiers had taken. Afranius and Petreius went to Pompey.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Spain came over to Caesar, including the legions with Varro, and Dio says his reputation and his cause profited from his clemency; he put no prisoner to death. Appian has him address the released men at the Varus, reminding them that he had spared them though Petreius had killed his men. Clemency had limits as policy: Dio says many of the men who fought against Caesar at Munda four years later had been captured with Afranius and Varro and spared.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Supply can decide a campaign without a pitched battle, but it nearly decided this one against Caesar when the floods cut him off. A commander who declines a battle he could win must carry his army with him: Caesar records the soldiers saying they would not fight later when he wanted them to. When the enemy's soldiers are fellow citizens who can talk to one's own, clemency works as a weapon.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Caesar's account is detailed and self-justifying; the reply he gives himself at the surrender is a political case against Pompey's long command in Spain. Appian tells it otherwise: Caesar was at first worsted and then fought an indecisive engagement, the men cut off by the broken bridge were destroyed by Petreius, and Caesar surrounded and released a division sent against his camp. Dio also has the cut-off men destroyed and says Caesar surrounded the retreating enemy with his superior numbers. Caesar says Plancus held out until relieved. The losses he gives for the fight at the mound and for the ambushed Gallic convoy are not repeated.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Caesar's Civil War 1.37–87, in A. G. Peskett's Loeb translation on LacusCurtius, is the main narrative. Appian's Civil Wars 2, Cassius Dio's Books 41 and 43 and Plutarch's Life of Caesar, in Loeb translations on LacusCurtius, give shorter later versions that differ on the opening fights. The 1911 Britannica's article on Caesar supplies the dates of his arrival and of the surrender.

phases.description: Caesar joins Fabius, offers battle below the Pompeian camp and entrenches close by.

phases.title: The mound and the flood
phases.description: The Afranians win the race for the mound; a flood breaks both of Caesar's bridges and hunger follows.

phases.title: The bridge upstream
phases.description: Boats carried overland put a legion across; a bridge restores supply and communities change sides.

phases.title: The race for the defiles
phases.description: Caesar's infantry fords the Sicoris, overtakes the column and reaches the hills before it.

phases.title: Water and surrender
phases.description: Cut off from the Ebro and from water, the Pompeians ask for terms and are disbanded.

perspectives.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
perspectives.objective: Remove Pompey's army in Spain before turning against Pompey, if possible without a battle.
perspectives.known: The strength of the position at Ilerda and the stores in the town; later, the enemy's intention to withdraw to the Ebro.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether Pompey was coming through Mauretania, as rumour said, and how long the floods would last.
perspectives.constraints: Rivers that could cut his communications, hunger in his camp and a country that at first favoured the enemy.
perspectives.forces: Veteran legions with Gallic cavalry and lightly armed Germans.
perspectives.terrain: Two rivers behind him and the rough hills and defiles between Ilerda and the Ebro.
perspectives.logistics: Fragile, dependent on bridges, allied communities and convoys from Gaul and Italy.
perspectives.decision: He outmarched the retreating enemy, cut them off from the Ebro and from water, and refused battle.
perspectives.outcome: The Pompeian army surrendered and was disbanded.

perspectives.name: Lucius Afranius and Marcus Petreius
perspectives.objective: Hold Ilerda, then withdraw into Celtiberia and prolong the war.
perspectives.known: Caesar's supply crisis after the floods; later, that he had bridged the river and won over the neighbouring communities.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether to march by night or by day, and whether their men would stay loyal.
perspectives.constraints: Divided counsel, soldiers talking with the enemy, and cavalry demoralised by Caesar's horse.
perspectives.forces: Pompey's legions in Spain with Spanish auxiliaries and cavalry.
perspectives.terrain: The strong position at Ilerda, then broken hills and dry country.
perspectives.logistics: Plentiful at first, through the bridge at Ilerda and the country beyond it; then cut off from water and fodder.
perspectives.decision: They withdrew toward the Ebro, postponed the march through the defiles and lost the race to them.
perspectives.outcome: They surrendered, their army was disbanded, and they went to Pompey.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Spain Caesar sailed from Brundisium for Epirus, on 4 January 48 BCE by the 1911 Britannica's date, running the blockade of Pompey's fleets. Suetonius says that when the rest of his troops were slow to follow, he tried to cross back alone at night in a small boat. Antony brought them over later. Pompey, who had raised a new army in the east, refused battle at Asparagium; Caesar then marched round by a long, difficult route and placed himself between Pompey and Dyrrhachium, where Pompey kept his stores and war material.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Caesar says he began to wall Pompey in for three reasons: to bring in supplies with less risk, since Pompey was stronger in cavalry; to stop Pompey foraging and make his cavalry useless; and to damage the prestige on which Pompey relied among foreign peoples, once it was known that he was besieged and dared not fight. Pompey held the sea and drew corn from Asia and every district he controlled; Plutarch says every wind brought him grain, troops or money while Caesar was reduced to straits by land and sea. The Livius article frames the stakes as monarchy, which Caesar eventually created, against a republic with a strong military leader.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Caesar aimed to enclose Pompey's army with a ring of forts and lines and force it to fight or starve. Pompey aimed to keep his base by the sea, to hold as wide a circle of hills as he could so that Caesar's lines were stretched, and to break out before the ring closed. He had decided not to fight a pitched battle at that time.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Dyrrhachium, at the start of the Via Egnatia to Thessalonica, was protected by broad swamps, according to the 1911 Britannica. Cut off from the town, Pompey camped on Petra, a height with a fair anchorage. The country around was hilly and rugged; Caesar fortified the heights and joined them with lines, and dammed or diverted the streams running to the sea. The southern end of his lines, by the sea, had a double rampart facing both ways, but the cross-wall that was to join the two along the shore was unfinished.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Pompey had the larger army, by Caesar's account, with a great superiority in cavalry and many archers and slingers, and command of the sea. Labienus, once Caesar's lieutenant in Gaul, served him. Caesar's veterans included the Ninth, which suffered badly in the fighting; Antony commanded on the lines, and Publius Sulla held the main camp in Caesar's absence. Two Allobrogian brothers, Raucillus and Egus, deserted from Caesar's cavalry after being accused of embezzling pay, and told Pompey where his lines were weak. Dio, unlike Caesar, says Caesar had the larger army.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The armies built facing rings: Caesar's outer line of forts and works around Pompey's positions, and Pompey's inner line of redoubts, which he completed faster because it was shorter and he had more men. Appian calls Caesar's plan an extremely difficult and chimerical task, undertaken because even failure would bring renown for its boldness.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: For weeks the armies fought for hills. Caesar's men lived on barley, meat and bread made from a root called chara, while the Pompeians' animals died and their men fell sick from the cramped space and the lack of water. In one day of six fights Sulla relieved a hard-pressed redoubt, whose defenders brought Caesar the arrows shot at it and the centurion Scaeva's shield. Then the deserters came. At dawn Pompey's men attacked the unfinished sea end of the lines from land and from boats and took the defenders from behind; Antony and then Caesar came up and halted them, but Pompey entrenched a new camp by the sea. Caesar's counterattack on an old camp, where a Pompeian legion had been seen, broke in and then collapsed when his right wing followed a wall to the river and Pompey came up with his legions. Caesar's men fled. The Livius article dates the breakout to 7 July by the Roman calendar.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Caesar chose to enclose an army larger than his own, in what he calls a new kind of warfare. Sulla, after relieving the redoubt, would not pursue; Caesar defends him, writing that a legate should act under direction and leave pitched battles to the commander. After the breakout Caesar attacked the isolated legion to repair the day's loss. After the defeat he gave up the lines, concentrated and marched away rather than fight with shaken troops and his corn supply in doubt. Plutarch says he spent that night reproaching himself for posting his army by a sea the enemy controlled instead of carrying the war into Macedonia and Thessaly.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The unfinished cross-wall at the sea, known to Pompey through the deserters, let his men land between Caesar's two ramparts and take the defenders in the rear. In the counterattack, the wall from the old camp to the river, which Caesar's right wing mistook for part of the camp, divided his force. Caesar observes that the same wall, by checking Pompey's pursuit, saved his army.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Caesar was beaten and lost many men, centurions and standards; Pompey was hailed imperator. By Caesar's account Labienus had the captured Caesarian soldiers paraded, mocked them as veterans who ran away, and killed them in front of the army. Caesar abandoned the siege and marched off toward Apollonia and then into Thessaly. The 1911 Britannica calls Dyrrhachium the place where Pompey made his last successful resistance to Caesar.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Pompeians, Caesar says, behaved as though they had already won and announced the victory throughout the world. Plutarch says Pompey still preferred to wear Caesar down by delay while Afranius urged him to recover Italy, and that his followers could no longer be restrained. Caesar's soldiers, ashamed, asked to be punished: Suetonius says their commander had rather to console than chastise them, and Appian that they demanded decimation, which he refused, punishing only a few standard-bearers. Within weeks the armies met at Pharsalus.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A blockade is only as strong as its weakest unfinished stretch, and deserters can find it. A commander who chooses the theatre must count who controls the sea: Plutarch's Caesar concluded that he had been besieged by want rather than besieging. Recovery after a defeat depended on the decision to break off at once and on an army that wanted to repair its disgrace.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Caesar says he enclosed a larger army with fewer men; Dio says he had the larger army. Caesar thinks Pompey did not follow up because he feared an ambush; Appian blames Labienus for persuading Pompey to chase the fugitives instead of taking Caesar's camp, and has Pompey hesitate. The saying that Pompey did not know how to use a victory survives in different words in Suetonius, in both of Plutarch's Lives and in Appian; Pompey's remark, on seeing the root bread, that he was fighting wild beasts is told by Suetonius and Appian; Plutarch has him hide the bread from his men, who already thought the enemy like wild beasts. None is an eyewitness report. Caesar, Plutarch and Appian give different numbers of standards and men lost, and these are not repeated.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Caesar's Civil War 3.41–75, in A. G. Peskett's Loeb translation on LacusCurtius, is the main narrative. Appian's Civil Wars 2, Cassius Dio's Book 41, Plutarch's Lives of Caesar and Pompey and Suetonius's Life of Julius Caesar, all in Loeb translations on LacusCurtius, give later versions. The Livius article by Jona Lendering gives a modern summary and the date, and the 1911 Britannica's articles on Durazzo and on Caesar give the setting.

phases.title: Race to Dyrrhachium
phases.description: Caesar marches round Pompey and cuts him off from his base; Pompey camps on Petra by the sea.

phases.title: The lines
phases.description: Forts and counter-forts on the hills; skirmishes, hunger in Caesar's army and thirst and sickness in Pompey's.

phases.title: Six fights in a day
phases.description: Pompey attacks several redoubts; Sulla relieves one, and the defenders' shields and arrows are brought to Caesar.

phases.title: The breakout
phases.description: Pompey storms the unfinished sea end of the lines by land and boat; Antony and Caesar halt the advance.

phases.title: Counterattack and rout
phases.description: Caesar's attack on the old camp breaks in, then collapses when Pompey arrives with his legions.

phases.title: Withdrawal
phases.description: Caesar sends his baggage to Apollonia and marches away; his cavalry checks the pursuit at the Genusus.

perspectives.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
perspectives.objective: Enclose Pompey's army and force it to fight or starve, while damaging his prestige abroad.
perspectives.known: Pompey's stores lay at Dyrrhachium, his cavalry was stronger, and his supplies came by sea.
perspectives.uncertainty: When his own fleets and supplies from Italy would arrive, and where Pompey would strike his long lines.
perspectives.constraints: Fewer men, by his account, to hold a far longer line, and an enemy fleet controlling the coast.
perspectives.forces: Veteran legions, including the Ninth, with cavalry and lightly armed troops.
perspectives.terrain: Rugged hills for his forts, streams he could dam, and a sea flank he had not finished closing.
perspectives.logistics: Corn scarce for weeks; barley, meat and root bread until the harvest ripened.
perspectives.decision: He built the ring, counterattacked after the breakout, and when that failed gave up the siege and marched away.
perspectives.outcome: He was defeated and withdrew into Thessaly, where he fought Pompey at Pharsalus weeks later.

perspectives.name: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (Pompey)
perspectives.objective: Keep his base and his communications by sea, avoid a pitched battle, and break the enclosing lines.
perspectives.known: From the Allobrogian deserters, the unfinished cross-wall at the sea end of Caesar's lines.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether Caesar's flight after the counterattack hid an ambush.
perspectives.constraints: Cramped ground within the lines, failing fodder for his horses and scarce water.
perspectives.forces: A larger army by Caesar's account, strong in cavalry, archers and slingers, with a fleet.
perspectives.terrain: Petra and the hills within the ring, and the sea at his back.
perspectives.logistics: Corn by sea from Asia and his other provinces; fodder had to come by sea from Corcyra and Acarnania.
perspectives.decision: He attacked the weak sea end by land and sea, then brought up his legions against Caesar's counterattack but did not press the pursuit.
perspectives.outcome: He broke the siege and was hailed imperator, but Caesar's army escaped intact.

Cassius Dio on the Battle of Pharsalus (41.52–63, trans. E. Cary)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Caesar crossed the Rubicon early in 49 BCE when the Senate would not let him stand for the consulship; Pompey fought for the Senate and withdrew from Italy to the east. In January 48 Caesar crossed the Adriatic. After months of opposing siege lines at Dyrrhachium he was defeated on 7 July and marched inland into Thessaly.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Pompey's camp held many senators. Plutarch says Pompey wanted to wear Caesar down by delay, but his followers mocked his caution and pressed for a decisive battle, and he gave way. Appian sets out Pompey's reasoning in full: his own supplies came by land and sea while Caesar's men had only what they could seize, so it was safer to reduce them by want than to risk everything on a battle with desperate veterans. He was overruled by the senators, knights and kings around him, some inexperienced, some elated by Dyrrhachium, some tired of the war, who accused him of delaying to prolong his command and called him “king of kings” and “Agamemnon”; against his will, Appian writes, he prepared for battle.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Caesar, short of supplies after Dyrrhachium, needed a battle; Pompey's best course was delay, which his own camp would not accept. The two commanders therefore had unequal reasons to fight. Appian says Caesar, approving Pompey's delays and not expecting a change, had sent three legions out to forage the night before, and recalled them with delight when he saw the enemy preparing to fight.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought near Pharsalus in Thessaly. Caesar says Pompey's right was covered by a river with steep banks. Scholars disagree whether the field lay north-west or north-east of the town; the author of the Livius article favours the north-east.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Caesar's account gives Pompey a much larger army than his own, and Dio says the Pompeians excelled in numbers and in cavalry and archers. Pompey's cavalry, archers and slingers were massed under Labienus. Caesar's veteran legions included the Tenth on his right and the Ninth, weakened at Dyrrhachium, on his left. Caesar's figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: In Caesar's account Pompey commanded his left with two legions Caesar had returned to the Senate, Scipio the centre, and the Cilician legion with Spanish cohorts the right by the river, with the cavalry massed on the left. Caesar placed Antony on his left, Domitius Calvinus in the centre and Sulla on the right. Expecting the cavalry to ride round his right, he took one cohort from each legion of his third line and formed a fourth line behind the right.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Livius dates the battle to 9 August 48 BCE. Pompey ordered his infantry to await the charge; Caesar's men, seeing them stand, halted midway, recovered their breath, then charged. Pompey's cavalry drove back Caesar's horse and began to outflank his line. The fourth line charged the cavalry, which fled, leaving the archers and slingers to be cut down, and then wheeled onto the Pompeian left from behind. Caesar committed his fresh third line, and the Pompeian army broke.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Caesar's decisive choice was to read Pompey's main effort and post a reserve against it. Pompey's order to stand and receive the charge was, in Caesar's judgement, a mistake that threw away the impetus of a charge. Plutarch says Caesar told the reserve cohorts to strike at the horsemen's faces.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The rout of the cavalry by the fourth line removed Pompey's main striking force and exposed his left wing to attack from the flank and rear.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Pompey rode back to his camp, which Caesar's men stormed, and escaped to Larisa and the coast. Plutarch, citing Asinius Pollio, who fought for Caesar that day, says Caesar looked on the Pompeian dead and said, “They would have it so”, and that most of those killed at the camp were servants. Pompeian troops who took refuge on a waterless hill surrendered and, in Caesar's account, were pardoned; Plutarch adds that Caesar took most of the captives into his legions and pardoned many prominent men, among them Brutus. Pompey sailed to Egypt, where King Ptolemy's advisers had him killed as he came ashore.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Livius calls the battle the end of the Roman Republic and the start of Caesar's autocracy. Dio says Caesar enrolled many captured soldiers in his own legions. Plutarch says Caesar, reaching Egypt after Pompey's death, had his murderers Achillas and Pothinus executed.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Anticipating the enemy's main effort and placing a reserve to meet it can defeat superior numbers. Cohorts detached from their legions gave Caesar the flexibility to build a new line during deployment.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Caesar's account is that of a participant defending his cause, and its figures favour him; Plutarch, citing Asinius Pollio, gives far lower Pompeian losses, and Appian too cites Pollio as one of Caesar's officers in the battle against what he calls exaggerating writers. Plutarch places Pompey on the right and Domitius with the cavalry on the left, where Caesar puts Pompey on the left, and he speaks of six reserve cohorts. Dio describes a long, even fight without a reserve and says Caesar executed captured senators, where Caesar stresses his clemency. Appian gives the fullest statement of Pompey's case for delay and blames the pressure of his followers and a divine infatuation for his decision to fight, a judgement as much literary as historical. The site is disputed. The figures in all these accounts are not repeated here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Caesar's Civil War 3.88–99, in the translation on Livius, is the main narrative. Plutarch's Life of Pompey draws on it, on Asinius Pollio and on others. Dio's account, also on Livius, is independent but rhetorical, with speeches and omens. Appian's Civil Wars 2 and Plutarch's Life of Caesar, both in the Loeb translations on LacusCurtius, add Pompey's reasoning and the pressure on him, and Pollio's testimony on the end of the battle.

phases.title: Dyrrhachium and retreat
phases.description: Caesar's siege lines fail at Dyrrhachium; he marches into Thessaly and Pompey follows.

phases.title: The fourth line
phases.description: Pompey masses cavalry on his left; Caesar forms a fourth line behind his right.

phases.title: Cavalry charge
phases.description: Pompey's cavalry turns Caesar's flank and is routed by the fourth line, which wheels onto the Pompeian left.

phases.title: Collapse and flight
phases.description: Caesar commits his third line; the Pompeian army breaks and the camp is stormed.

perspectives.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
perspectives.objective: Bring Pompey to battle and destroy his army before supply problems wore down his own.
perspectives.known: Pompey's cavalry, archers and slingers were massed opposite his right.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether his own small cavalry force could hold off Pompey's horse.
perspectives.constraints: His army was outnumbered and short of supplies after Dyrrhachium.
perspectives.forces: Veteran legions, including the Tenth and the weakened Ninth, and a smaller cavalry force.
perspectives.terrain: A plain near Pharsalus, with Pompey's right covered by a river.
perspectives.logistics: After his defeat at Dyrrhachium he had marched inland, Plutarch says for lack of supplies.
perspectives.decision: He formed a fourth line from his third-line cohorts behind his right and held the third line in reserve.
perspectives.outcome: Pompey's army broke and Pompey fled to Egypt.

perspectives.name: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (Pompey)
perspectives.objective: Plutarch and Appian say he preferred to wear Caesar down by delay, since his own supplies were secure and Caesar's were not, rather than risk battle with desperate veterans.
perspectives.known: His army and cavalry were much larger than Caesar's.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether his less experienced troops could beat Caesar's veterans in open battle.
perspectives.constraints: Senators, knights and kings in his camp pressed for an immediate battle and accused him of prolonging the war to keep his command.
perspectives.forces: Legions including two that Caesar had returned, Syrian and Cilician legions, Spanish cohorts, and a large force of cavalry, archers and slingers.
perspectives.terrain: A river protecting his right flank.
perspectives.logistics: Better supplied than Caesar, which made delay a realistic option.
perspectives.decision: He massed cavalry under Labienus to turn Caesar's right and ordered his infantry to await the charge.
perspectives.outcome: His cavalry was routed, his army broke and he was killed in Egypt.

A. G. Way, Introduction to The Spanish War (Loeb Classical Library, 1955)
Cassius Dio, Roman History, Book 43 (Loeb translation)
Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar (Loeb translation)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Thapsus in April 46 BCE the Pompeian cause survived in Further Spain, where Gnaeus Pompeius, Pompey's elder son, raised an army and his brother Sextus held Corduba. The 1911 Britannica says Caesar was obliged to sail for Spain in November. The campaign that followed was a winter of sieges and marches around Ategua, Ucubi and Ventipo; as towns fell to Caesar, Dio writes, other communities came over to him, and Pompeius moved from place to place.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Plutarch says the sons of Pompey were young but had gathered an army of amazing size and showed a boldness that justified their claim to lead. Dio says many of their soldiers had been captured with Afranius and Varro, spared, handed over to Longinus and had then revolted from him, so that they had nothing to hope for if beaten. It was a war of Romans against Romans, with Spanish and Moorish allies on both sides; Plutarch adds that the triumph Caesar celebrated for it vexed the Romans as nothing else had, because it marked the destruction of the family of the greatest Roman.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Pompeius, by the anonymous author's account, had written to the people of Ursao that Caesar would not come down into the valley because most of his army was inexperienced, and offered battle from ground protected by the hills and by the town. Caesar, about to march on, raised the signal for battle when his scouts reported the enemy in line. Dio says Pompeius chose to risk a battle because he feared that his remaining adherents would desert him.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: A plain ran between the camps. Near the town the ground rose, and a stream crossed the plain with marshy, broken ground on its right, which made the approach awkward for Caesar's troops; the Pompeian line stood on the slope in front of the town wall. The site of Munda is disputed. The Loeb editor, A. G. Way, follows Holmes and Veith in placing it a few miles north-west of Ursao, the modern Osuna; Stoffel and Klotz put it at Montilla, and Hübner at a place known locally as Campo de Munda.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Both armies had citizen legions with native troops and Moors: the sons of the Moorish king Bocchus fought for Pompeius, and King Bogud with Caesar. Caesar's army mixed veteran and newly raised legions, with the Tenth on the right and the Third and Fifth on the left. Titus Labienus and Attius Varus served Pompeius. The anonymous author gives the strength of both armies; the figures are not repeated.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Pompeius kept his line close to the town and the high ground. Caesar expected him to come down into the plain and advanced; when his men reached the stream and the broken ground at the far edge of the plain, they found the enemy waiting above them. Caesar began to restrict the advance, and his men, the author says, were bitterly disgusted, thinking their chance of victory was being taken from them.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The battle was joined with shouting and volleys so fierce that, the author admits, Caesar's men nearly lost confidence. The Tenth on the right pressed the enemy back until Pompeius moved a legion from his right to support his left; Caesar's cavalry then attacked so that the line could not be reinforced, and the Pompeians broke and fled to the town and their camp. Dio describes the allies on both sides fleeing early while the legions fought it out, both commanders dismounting to join the fight, and the break coming when Labienus left his post to meet King Bogud's move against the Pompeian camp, and the Pompeians took it for flight. Survivors who reached Munda were blockaded behind a rampart of weapons and bodies.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Caesar accepted battle on ground his enemy had chosen, then limited the advance up the slope; Way suggests that he did not yet know the strength of the prepared positions. When the fight hung in the balance he went into the ranks. Plutarch has him run through the lines asking his men whether they were not ashamed to hand him over to boys; Dio says both commanders leapt from their horses and fought. On the Pompeian side, the transfer of a legion across the line and Labienus's departure from his station each weakened the front at the moment of greatest pressure.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The two narratives explain the collapse differently. The anonymous author makes it the pressure of the Tenth, which forced Pompeius to shift a legion, and the cavalry attack that stopped him reinforcing the line. Dio makes it Labienus's move against Bogud, which the Pompeian ranks read as flight.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Pompeians were routed on 17 March 45 BCE, the day of the Liberalia; Labienus and Attius Varus were killed. Munda was blockaded and later taken. Sextus Pompeius left Corduba by night; Gnaeus, wounded, was carried to Carteia, failed to escape by sea and was later killed. Plutarch says his head was brought to Caesar by Deidius; Dio that he was defeated by Caesennius Lento and died in a wood.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Caesar took Corduba and Hispalis; Dio says he killed the armed slaves at Corduba and sold the rest, levied tribute so rigorously that he took the offerings in the temple of Hercules at Gades, and rewarded the cities that had favoured him with land, exemptions and citizenship. The 1911 Britannica records that he returned to Rome in September and was murdered six months later. Plutarch calls Munda the last war Caesar waged.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An attack uphill against a prepared line relied on the quality of the attacking troops, and on this day it nearly failed. Soldiers who expect no mercy fight to the end: Dio connects the Pompeians' resistance to the fate they feared after being spared once already. In a battle this even, a misread movement behind the line could decide it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The Spanish War was attached to Caesar's name but its author is unknown; Way judges him an honest man struggling with an unfamiliar task, whose colloquial grammar and habit of changing the subject without warning cause serious ambiguities, so that even which enemy wing Caesar's cavalry attacked depends on the reading of the manuscripts. Dio's account is rhetorical and opens with omens. Plutarch reports Caesar saying after the battle that he had often fought for victory but now for the first time for his life; Suetonius says that, believing the battle lost, he thought of suicide. Neither names a witness. The casualty figures in the Spanish War and in Plutarch are not repeated, and the site of Munda is still disputed.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Spanish War, in A. G. Way's Loeb translation on LacusCurtius with his introduction and notes, is the only detailed narrative. Cassius Dio's Book 43, Plutarch's Life of Caesar and Suetonius's Life of Julius Caesar, also in Loeb translations on LacusCurtius, give later versions. The 1911 Britannica's article on Caesar supplies the frame of the campaign.
