phases.description: Caesar takes Ategua and Ventipo; Pompeius burns Ucubi and moves from position to position.

phases.title: The armies meet
phases.description: Caesar camps opposite Pompeius in the plain of Munda.

phases.title: Battle on the slope
phases.description: Caesar's men advance to the stream and climb against the Pompeian line; the fight hangs in the balance.

phases.title: The break
phases.description: The Tenth presses the Pompeian left, the cavalry attacks, and the Pompeian line breaks.

phases.title: The town and the pursuit
phases.description: Munda is blockaded and taken; Sextus flees Corduba, and Gnaeus is hunted down and killed.

perspectives.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
perspectives.objective: Destroy the last Pompeian army in the field.
perspectives.known: His scouts reported that Pompeius had stood in battle order since the third watch, on ground protected by the town and the hills.
perspectives.uncertainty: The strength of the enemy's prepared positions on the heights.
perspectives.constraints: An army that mixed veterans with recruits, and broken ground beyond the stream.
perspectives.forces: Veteran and new legions, cavalry, and King Bogud's Moors.
perspectives.terrain: A plain crossed by a stream with marshy ground, rising to the slope in front of the town.
perspectives.logistics: He was campaigning in a province held by his enemies, sustained by the towns he took and the communities that came over to him.
perspectives.decision: He accepted battle, limited the advance up the slope, and then went into the ranks himself.
perspectives.outcome: The Pompeian army was destroyed, and he took Munda, Corduba and Hispalis.

perspectives.name: Gnaeus Pompeius, son of Pompey
perspectives.objective: Defeat Caesar on ground of his own choosing before his support in Spain fell away.
perspectives.known: He believed, or told his allies, that Caesar would not come down to fight because his army was inexperienced.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether his men would hold against Caesar's veterans in open battle.
perspectives.constraints: Communities deserting him after Caesar's sieges, and soldiers with nothing to hope for if defeated.
perspectives.forces: Legions that included men once captured with Afranius and Varro and others who had revolted from Longinus, with Spanish and Moorish allies, Labienus and Attius Varus.
perspectives.terrain: The slope in front of the town of Munda, with the town behind him.
perspectives.logistics: The towns of Baetica that still held for him, and Munda as a refuge.
perspectives.decision: He offered battle from the heights and stayed close to the town rather than advance into the plain.
perspectives.outcome: His army was routed; he escaped wounded and was killed in the pursuit.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Caesar's murder, Antony and Octavian defeated the assassins at Philippi in 42 BCE and divided the empire. Antony took the East, where he allied with Cleopatra VII of Egypt, and relations with Octavian deteriorated.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Octavian used a document, probably forged in Livius's view, suggesting that Antony meant to give Roman land to Cleopatra. The Senate declared war on Cleopatra and stripped Antony of his powers. Livius notes that Octavian's annexation of Dalmatia gave him a land route to the Balkans.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Antony intended to cross to Italy, but Octavian moved first, landing in Epirus and establishing himself at the Gulf of Ambracia while Agrippa cut Antony's sea communications from the south. Plutarch says Antony, though stronger on land, insisted on a decision at sea to please Cleopatra.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Antony's fleet lay inside the Ambracian Gulf, whose narrow mouth is flanked by the promontory of Actium to the south. Antony camped on Actium and bridged to the northern promontory; Octavian's camp there later became Nicopolis. The battle was fought off the gulf's mouth in the afternoon, when northerly winds favoured a breakout to the south.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Antony had large, heavy warships carrying soldiers and archers; Plutarch says his crews were short and poorly trained, while Octavian's lighter ships were well manned. Agrippa, whom Octavian regarded as the better commander, led the fleet. The ancient fleet and army sizes are paper strengths and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Octavian and Agrippa strengthened their wings so as not to be outflanked; Antony aimed his main attack through his own centre. Before the battle Antony burned most of the Egyptian ships, keeping sixty, and had sails carried aboard.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Agrippa's seizure of bases in the western Peloponnese and at Patras cut Antony's supply lines, and hunger wore down his army; allies such as Domitius, Amyntas and Deiotarus deserted. On 2 September 31 BCE the fleets engaged off the gulf. In Dio's account Antony's fleet drew up in dense array just outside the strait and waited; when Octavian bent his line into a crescent to envelop it, Antony advanced to meet him, and the lighter Caesarian ships fought the heavy Antonian galleys like cavalry against heavy infantry, ramming and backing off under showers of stones and arrows. Antony's centre broke through Agrippa's centre, Cleopatra's sixty ships passed through the gap and sailed south, and Antony followed with his own squadron.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Antony chose to break out by sea rather than retreat overland, as Canidius advised. Octavian refused battle while the blockade did its work. Cassius Dio describes the decision on the Antonian side: after a naval reverse and a defeat of his cavalry, and with provisions failing, Antony held a council, and Cleopatra's advice prevailed, to garrison the strongest positions and take the rest back to Egypt. Not wishing to seem to flee and so frighten their allies, they prepared the breakout as if for a naval battle, burning the ships they could not man and loading their treasure by night. Dio says Octavian at first meant to let them slip past and attack their rear, until Agrippa persuaded him that their sails would outrun him.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The departure of Cleopatra and Antony left the remaining fleet without its commander. Plutarch says it fought on until late afternoon before giving up; Dio, whom Livius follows, says that as the fight stayed even Octavian sent to his camp for fire, which he had avoided in the hope of taking the treasure, and that the lighter ships then set the large galleys ablaze with flaming missiles and pots of burning pitch.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Antony's army waited seven days and then, deserted by Canidius, went over to Octavian, who offered favourable terms. Antony and Cleopatra reached Egypt.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: In 30 BCE Octavian pursued them to Egypt, and both killed themselves as he besieged Alexandria. Octavian, as Augustus, ruled alone for over forty years. He founded Nicopolis on the site of his camp and commemorated the victory as a war against a foreign queen.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: The battle was largely decided by the blockade that preceded it: supply, morale and the loyalty of allies had collapsed before the fleets met. Livius argues that the breakout was a tactical success that brought strategic ruin, because the army was left behind.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Whether the escape was a planned breakout or a flight is debated: Livius treats it as a breakout that succeeded, while Plutarch presents Cleopatra's flight and Antony's pursuit of her as desertion of his men. Dio's narrative supports both readings: he describes the breakout as planned in council and disguised as preparation for battle, yet says Cleopatra, unable to bear the suspense, fled and that Antony followed believing her ships were beaten, and he explains her flight by her nature “as a woman and an Egyptian”, the hostile tradition at its plainest. Augustan propaganda, visible in Virgil and in monuments such as the Palestrina relief, cast the civil war as a foreign war and shaped later accounts. Plutarch's fleet and army figures are not repeated.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Plutarch's Life of Antony and Cassius Dio's Roman History 50, in the Loeb translation on LacusCurtius, are the main narratives; Dio gives the Antonian council, Octavian's plans and the use of fire. Livius summarises Dio 50.32–35 and treats Virgil's Aeneid 8 and the commemorative monuments as evidence of propaganda.

phases.title: Blockade
phases.description: Agrippa cuts Antony's supply lines; hunger and desertion weaken his army at Actium.

phases.title: Preparing the breakout
phases.description: Antony burns surplus ships and prepares to force a passage by sea.

phases.title: Through the centre
phases.description: Antony's centre breaks through; Cleopatra's squadron and then Antony sail south.

phases.title: Surrender
phases.description: The remaining fleet is destroyed or surrenders; the army goes over to Octavian after seven days.

perspectives.name: Octavian and Agrippa
perspectives.objective: Destroy Antony's power without fighting on unequal terms.
perspectives.known: Antony's army was going hungry and his allies were wavering.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether and when Antony would try to break out by sea or by land.
perspectives.constraints: Antony was the stronger on land.
perspectives.forces: Lighter, well-manned warships under Agrippa, and the legions in the camp on the northern promontory.
perspectives.terrain: The narrow mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, which Antony had to pass.
perspectives.logistics: Bases in the Peloponnese and at Patras that cut Antony's sea routes.
perspectives.decision: They refused battle while the blockade worked; Octavian thought of letting the enemy slip past to attack their rear until Agrippa dissuaded him, then they strengthened their wings, bent their line to envelop the enemy and finally used fire.
perspectives.outcome: Antony and Cleopatra escaped, but their fleet was destroyed and their army surrendered.

perspectives.name: Mark Antony
perspectives.objective: Break out of the gulf and preserve his cause.
perspectives.known: His army was being worn down by hunger and allies were deserting.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether his army could follow by land once the fleet had escaped.
perspectives.constraints: Short-handed and poorly trained crews, in Plutarch's account, and Cleopatra's insistence on a sea battle.
perspectives.forces: Large warships carrying soldiers and archers, Cleopatra's squadron with the treasury, and a large army under Canidius.
perspectives.terrain: A gulf whose mouth his fleet had to force.
perspectives.logistics: Supply lines cut by Agrippa; Cleopatra's ships carried the treasury.
perspectives.decision: On Cleopatra's advice in council he chose to break out to Egypt, disguised the breakout as preparation for battle, burned surplus ships, attacked through the centre and followed Cleopatra when she broke away.
perspectives.outcome: He escaped to Egypt but lost his fleet, his army and, in 30 BCE, his life.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Rome had campaigned east of the Rhine since Drusus reached the Elbe in 9 BCE, and Tiberius renewed the conquest in 4–5 CE. Varus, a senator and friend of Augustus, governed the land between the Lower Rhine and the Lower Elbe with the aim of turning it into a regular province.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Dio says Varus pressed harder to change local customs and demanded tribute as from subjects, which the leaders resented; Velleius portrays a governor who thought Germans could be ruled by law rather than the sword. Arminius, a Cheruscan noble with Roman equestrian rank, was among his trusted companions.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Arminius aimed to draw the army away from its bases into ground where it could not fight in formation. Varus meant to deal with a reported rising; Livius reconstructs his route north-west toward the Ems and the army's later turn toward the Rhine.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Part of the fighting took place at Kalkriese, north of modern Osnabrück, where a strip of solid ground about 220 metres wide runs between the Kalkrieser Berg and a great bog, and the slope was fortified. Livius argues that the Latin saltus means narrows rather than forest, and treats Dio's steep ravines and dense trees as a literary convention.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Varus led three legions, the Seventeenth, Eighteenth and Nineteenth, with cavalry and auxiliary cohorts, encumbered by wagons, animals, women, children and servants. Arminius's coalition fought with javelins, spears and shields, and grew as wavering groups joined it.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Velleius and Dio say Varus was warned of the plot, by Segestes according to Velleius, and refused to believe it. The conspirators asked leave to gather allied forces, then killed the Roman detachments in their communities and attacked the column on the march.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Dio describes several days of fighting. The Romans camped and burned or abandoned their wagons, reached open country with losses, and were attacked again in woods where cavalry and infantry collided; rain and wind soaked their shields and bows. On the fourth day, in Dio's account, Varus and his senior officers killed themselves and resistance collapsed. Livius reconstructs the route from near Minden past Kalkriese toward the Ems.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: As the sources tell it, Varus's decisive errors were to ignore the warning and to march a column with its baggage into hostile country on the strength of Arminius's report. Velleius says the cavalry commander Vala Numonius abandoned the infantry and the camp prefect Ceionius proposed surrender.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: At Kalkriese the column, unable to form ranks among its wagons and noncombatants, was attacked from the fortified slope and, on Livius's reading of the finds, cut in two.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The three legions were destroyed. Captured officers were sacrificed; other captives were enslaved, and some were later ransomed. Varus's body was mutilated and his head sent to Maroboduus and then to Augustus. One fortress, probably Haltern, held out.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Dio says Augustus feared an invasion of Italy and levied troops. Tiberius secured the Rhine. Germanicus campaigned beyond it from 14 to 16 CE, buried the dead on the battlefield and recovered an eagle, but Tiberius chose not to occupy Germania east of the Rhine.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Reliance on a trusted informant, combined with a long baggage-laden column in difficult country, turned a political misjudgement into a military disaster. The defeat showed the limits of Roman power rather than ending it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Whether Kalkriese is the main battlefield or one episode is debated; Livius treats it as the scene of the first major attack. Florus has Varus summon Arminius, where Velleius and Dio have him reject the warning. Velleius knew some of those involved and writes with a pro-Roman, pro-Tiberian slant. Livius argues that Rome's decision not to reconquer Germania was a choice that predated the defeat, and that nineteenth-century nationalism inflated the battle's meaning.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The literary sources are Velleius Paterculus, an officer of the period, Cassius Dio 56.18–24, and the passages of Tacitus and Florus discussed by Livius. Livius's multi-part reconstruction combines them with the archaeology at Kalkriese.

phases.title: The warning ignored
phases.description: Varus dismisses the warning and marches to deal with a reported rising.

phases.title: Ambush on the march
phases.description: The conspirators leave the column; at Kalkriese it is attacked from a fortified slope and split.

phases.title: Open country and woods
phases.description: The Romans burn their wagons, reach open ground and are caught again in woodland.

phases.title: Storm and collapse
phases.description: In rain and wind Varus and his officers kill themselves and the army disintegrates.

perspectives.name: Publius Quinctilius Varus
perspectives.objective: Turn Germania into a regular province and suppress a reported rising.
perspectives.known: Arminius, a trusted officer, reported unrest among distant peoples.
perspectives.uncertainty: Velleius and Dio say he was warned of a plot but did not believe it.
perspectives.constraints: His troops had been dispersed among communities, and the march carried a heavy baggage train.
perspectives.forces: Three legions, cavalry and auxiliaries, with wagons and noncombatants.
perspectives.terrain: Marsh, forest and narrow strips of solid ground.
perspectives.logistics: A long column building roads and bridges as it went.
perspectives.decision: He ignored the warning and marched the army, with its baggage, toward the reported rising.
perspectives.outcome: His army was destroyed and he killed himself.

perspectives.name: Arminius
perspectives.objective: Destroy the Roman army and end Roman rule east of the Rhine.
perspectives.known: Varus's plans and routes, as one of his trusted companions.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the Romans would believe the reported rising and leave their known routes.
perspectives.constraints: His warriors were lightly armed and could not beat legions in formation or storm a fortified camp.
perspectives.forces: A coalition led by the Cherusci that grew as other groups joined after early successes.
perspectives.terrain: Narrows between hill and bog, which his men fortified.
perspectives.logistics: Local knowledge and support among communities hostile to Roman tribute.
perspectives.decision: He reported a distant rising, left the column with his allies and attacked the army on the march over several days.
perspectives.outcome: Three legions were destroyed and Germania remained outside the empire.

sources.title: Boudica's Defeat
sources.publisher: Warwick Classics Network, University of Warwick

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Claudius invaded Britain in 43 CE. By about 60 the governor Suetonius Paulinus was campaigning in the west and attacked the island of Mona (Anglesey), where Britons and Druids resisted.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: When the Icenian king Prasutagus died, leaving Nero co-heir with his daughters, his kingdom was plundered, his widow Boudica was flogged and his daughters raped, according to Tacitus. The Iceni rose, and the Trinovantes joined them, angry at the veterans of the colony at Camulodunum who had seized their land.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The rebels sought revenge and the destruction of Roman power in the province. Paulinus needed to concentrate a force and fight on ground of his own choosing before the revolt spread further.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battlefield is unknown. Proposals include a point on Watling Street near High Cross, Mancetter (Manduessedum), sites nearer Coventry, Arbury Banks and Church Stowe. Tacitus describes a narrow defile with woods behind the Roman line and an open plain in front.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Paulinus had the Fourteenth Legion, a detachment of the Twentieth and auxiliaries; the camp prefect of the Second, Poenius Postumus, did not join him. The British host was far larger, armed with long swords, spears and shields and mostly without armour. Tacitus's and Dio's figures are not credible and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Paulinus placed the legionaries in close order in the centre, light troops on the flanks and cavalry on the wings. The Britons, confident of victory, brought their families in wagons to watch from the edge of the plain.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The rebels sacked Camulodunum, whose temple held out for two days, and routed the Ninth Legion under Petilius Cerialis. Paulinus marched to Londinium, judged it indefensible and left it with its people; Londinium and Verulamium were destroyed and their inhabitants killed. In the battle the legionaries held the defile until the Britons had spent their missiles, then advanced in a wedge with the auxiliaries and cavalry.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Paulinus's decisive choices were to abandon Londinium, sacrificing its people to preserve his army, and to accept battle only on ground that narrowed the British front and protected his flanks and rear.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Once the British attack was spent, the Roman wedge drove into the crowded host. In the narrow ground the Britons could not use their long swords, and their own wagons blocked their retreat.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Tacitus says no quarter was given, even to women. Boudica died by poison in Tacitus's account and of illness in Dio's. Poenius Postumus killed himself.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Reinforcements came from Germany and the army harried hostile tribes; famine followed because the Britons had not sown their crops. The procurator Classicianus urged a milder policy, and Paulinus was replaced by Petronius Turpilianus, who avoided conflict. The Fourteenth Legion received the title Martia Victrix.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Terrain that narrows the frontage can let a disciplined smaller force defeat a much larger one, and a crowd without a line of retreat is vulnerable once checked. The revolt's origins show how misgovernment can create a military crisis.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The site and the year are uncertain: Tacitus places the revolt in 61 CE, while the Encyclopaedia Romana judges 60 more likely. The ancient figures for the dead in the towns and in the battle are not credible, as the Warwick page notes. Tacitus and Dio disagree on Boudica's death, and Tacitus writes from a Roman perspective that emphasizes Roman superiority.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Tacitus's Annals 14.29–39 is the main narrative. The Warwick Classics Network page, adapted from Caitlin Gillespie's study of Boudica, reviews the location debate and the reliability of the figures; the Encyclopaedia Romana summarizes Dio's alternative account, which was not read directly.

phases.title: Mona and the revolt
phases.description: Paulinus attacks Mona as the Iceni and Trinovantes rise behind him.

phases.title: The towns destroyed
phases.description: Camulodunum falls, the Ninth is routed, and Londinium and Verulamium are abandoned and destroyed.

phases.title: Choosing the ground
phases.description: Paulinus concentrates his army in a defile with woods behind and open ground in front.

phases.title: Wedge and rout
phases.description: The legions hold, then advance in a wedge; the wagons trap the fleeing Britons.

perspectives.name: Gaius Suetonius Paulinus
perspectives.objective: Destroy the rebel army before the revolt spread further.
perspectives.known: The towns had fallen and the Ninth Legion had been defeated.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the Second Legion would join him; it did not.
perspectives.constraints: A small force far from reinforcement, facing a much larger host.
perspectives.forces: The Fourteenth Legion, a detachment of the Twentieth and auxiliaries.
perspectives.terrain: A defile with woods behind and an open plain in front.
perspectives.logistics: Cut off from the abandoned towns; reinforcements from Germany came only after the battle.
perspectives.decision: He abandoned Londinium and fought only on ground that narrowed the British front.
perspectives.outcome: The rebel army was destroyed, but his harsh policy afterwards led to his replacement.

perspectives.name: Boudica
perspectives.objective: Avenge the outrages against her family and people and drive out Roman rule.
perspectives.known: The colony, Londinium and Verulamium had fallen and a legion had been beaten.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether a host of many peoples could beat a disciplined Roman army in open battle.
perspectives.constraints: Her forces were numerous but largely unarmoured and loosely organized, with families present.
perspectives.forces: Warriors of the Iceni, Trinovantes and their allies, with chariots, spears and long swords.
perspectives.terrain: An open plain leading into the defile the Romans held.
perspectives.logistics: Wagons carrying families followed the army; famine later followed the neglected harvest.
perspectives.decision: She attacked the Roman position head-on.
perspectives.outcome: Her army was destroyed and she died soon after, by poison in Tacitus's account.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: A revolt against Roman rule broke out in Judaea in 66 CE and defeated Legion XII Fulminata that year. Vespasian reduced Galilee in 67, taking Jotapata. In 69 he was proclaimed emperor and left the war to his son Titus, with the former governor Tiberius Julius Alexander as his chief of staff.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Rival factions held Jerusalem. Eleazar son of Simon's Zealots held the Temple until John of Gischala seized it at Passover; Simon bar Giora held the upper city. Tacitus says the factions fought and betrayed one another and burned large stores of grain, uniting only as the Romans approached, while refugees from captured towns crowded into the city.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Titus needed to take the city and end the revolt; Tacitus says the push for an early assault came partly from the soldiers' hope of plunder and Titus's own ambition. The defenders, divided in their aims, trusted to the city's walls and the fortified Temple. Livius credits Vespasian with a strategy of letting the factions weaken one another first.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Jerusalem stood on hills above steep valleys, enclosed by successive walls with towers. Herod's palace and the Antonia fortress overlooked the city, and the Temple was itself built like a fortress, with its own walls and colonnades, a spring and cisterns.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Titus had the Fifth, Tenth, Twelfth and Fifteenth legions with detachments of others, auxiliaries from client kingdoms, Arab troops and veterans; Josephus served him as adviser and interpreter. The defenders were divided among the followers of John, Simon and Eleazar. Tacitus's figure for the besieged is not credible and is not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Titus began the siege at Passover, on 14 April 70 CE. The legions camped north-east of the city and on the Mount of Olives, then moved camps to the west. Because the ground ruled out a quick assault, Titus prepared siege works.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Rams and siege towers broke the first wall in May and the second soon after. Ramps against the Antonia were undermined and burned, and Titus then enclosed the city with a wall to starve it. The Antonia fell in early July and was demolished; the daily sacrifice ended in mid-July. The Temple burned on 10 August, and the upper city fell on 8 September.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Titus's decisive choice was to turn from assault to blockade, enclosing the city and cutting down the trees for a wide radius, so that famine would do what the rams could not. Josephus has him hold a council on the Temple and argue for sparing it. The factions refused repeated calls to surrender.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The fall of the Antonia gave the Romans access to the Temple platform. Once the Temple was burning, organized resistance there collapsed.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The city and its Temple were destroyed. The famine was so severe that, in a surviving fragment of Tacitus, the dead lay unburied in the streets and the starving ate whatever they could, including human flesh. Livius reports that people caught outside the walls were crucified in great numbers, that starving people who surrendered died, and that some were cut open by soldiers searching for swallowed coins. After the fall, many inhabitants were killed; survivors were enslaved, executed or sent to forced labour.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Vespasian and Titus celebrated a triumph in Rome, after which Simon bar Giora was executed; John of Gischala was imprisoned for life. The Temple's treasures paid for coins proclaiming Judaea captured, the Menorah was displayed in Rome, and captives were forced to work on building projects including the Colosseum. Jews throughout the empire had to pay a special tax, the fiscus Judaicus. Masada fell in 73 or 74.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Systematic siegecraft, from towers and rams to ramps and finally a blockade, overcame strong fortifications, at the price of deliberately starving a city's population. Internal division weakened the defence long before the Romans arrived.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Who decided the Temple's fate is disputed. Josephus, an eyewitness in Titus's service, says a soldier set it alight against Titus's wishes; Livius doubts this and notes that the Christian writer Sulpicius Severus, whose account he traces to Tacitus, has Titus order the destruction, as does a fragment printed with Tacitus's Histories. The figures given by Josephus and Tacitus for the population and the dead are not credible and are not repeated. Tacitus's account of Jewish origins and customs is hostile and inaccurate.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Josephus's Jewish War, in Whiston's translation, is the eyewitness narrative; only the passages on the council and the burning of the Temple were read here. Tacitus's Histories describe the city and the opening of the siege, and the fragments the famine and the council. Livius's articles reconstruct the siege, date its stages and weigh the sources.

phases.title: Encirclement
phases.description: Titus encamps at Passover; the factions inside unite only as the legions arrive.

phases.title: The outer walls
phases.description: Rams and siege towers break the first and second walls.

phases.title: Famine and the Antonia
phases.description: Ramps fail and a wall encloses the city to starve it; the Antonia falls in early July.

phases.title: Temple and upper city
phases.description: The Temple burns; the upper city falls and its people are killed or enslaved.

perspectives.name: Titus
perspectives.objective: Take Jerusalem and end the revolt.
perspectives.known: The city was divided among rival factions and crowded with refugees.
perspectives.uncertainty: How long the walls and the fortified Temple could hold.
perspectives.constraints: Strong fortifications on hills, and soldiers Tacitus describes as eager for plunder.
perspectives.forces: Four legions with detachments, auxiliaries and allied troops.
perspectives.terrain: Hills, valleys and successive walls, with the Antonia and the fortified Temple.
perspectives.logistics: Timber for siege works, cut until none was left for a wide radius around the city.
perspectives.decision: He broke the outer walls, then enclosed the city to starve it before storming the Antonia and the Temple.
perspectives.outcome: The city and Temple were destroyed, and he celebrated a triumph in Rome.

perspectives.name: John of Gischala and Simon bar Giora
perspectives.objective: Hold the city and Temple against Rome.
perspectives.known: The Romans had reduced the rest of the country and encamped around the city.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the walls and the Temple could outlast the siege.
perspectives.constraints: Their factions had fought each other and burned grain stores before the siege.
perspectives.forces: Rival armed followings, together with the Zealots who had followed Eleazar.
perspectives.terrain: Successive walls, the Antonia and the Temple.
perspectives.logistics: Stores reduced by their own conflict; famine set in once the Roman wall closed the city.
perspectives.decision: They refused to surrender, undermined and burned the Roman ramps and fought on from the Temple.
perspectives.outcome: John surrendered and was imprisoned; Simon was captured and executed in Rome.

sources.title: Lactantius, Of the Manner in Which the Persecutors Died 44 (trans. W. Fletcher)
Eusebius, Life of Constantine 1.26–40 (trans. E. C. Richardson)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Diocletian's Tetrarchy shared rule among two senior and two junior emperors. When Constantius I died in 306, his army proclaimed his son Constantine at York, while in Rome the Senate and the Praetorian Guard proclaimed Maxentius, son of Maximian. The other rulers declared Maxentius a usurper.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Maxentius held Italy and Africa. In 311, after Galerius's death, he declared war on Constantine, blaming him for his father's death, and stationed an army at Verona. Constantine allied with Licinius in the East.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Constantine meant to take Italy and Africa. Maxentius at first intended to wait behind Rome's walls and cut the bridges over the Tiber to slow the invader.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Via Flaminia approached Rome from the north and crossed the Tiber at the Milvian Bridge. Maxentius had cut that bridge, then built a pontoon bridge some distance away to bring his army across to the north bank, where it fought with the river behind it.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Constantine crossed the Alps with his field army. Lactantius says Maxentius had the larger army, drawn from his father's troops and from Mauretania and Italy. Casualties on both sides are unknown.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 28 October 312 Maxentius's army crossed by the pontoon bridge and deployed facing Constantine north of the river. Lactantius says Constantine had camped opposite the Milvian Bridge.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Constantine took Turin and Milan and defeated the army at Verona together with a relief force, then marched on Rome. Unrest grew in the city. Maxentius consulted the Sibylline books, which seemed to promise that the enemy of the Romans would die that day, and marched out on the anniversary of his accession. Constantine's army broke Maxentius's, and the fugitives overloaded the bridge.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Maxentius's decision to leave the walls of Rome and fight with a river at his back proved decisive. Lactantius attributes it to unrest in the city and the oracle; Eusebius describes the bridge of boats as a trap Maxentius had set. Both describe a Christian sign adopted by Constantine before the battle.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: When Maxentius's army broke, its only line of retreat was the bridge, and the crush of fugitives brought it down.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Maxentius fell into the Tiber and drowned. Constantine entered Rome the next day; Maxentius's body was recovered and his head sent to Carthage, and Africa surrendered.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Constantine ruled the West. In 313 he and Licinius issued the Edict of Milan, tolerating Christianity, and Constantine favoured the Church. After defeating Licinius in 324 he ruled the whole empire and moved the capital to Constantinople. Maxentius's memory was condemned.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Giving up a fortified position to fight in the open, with a river behind and a single fragile line of retreat, turned defeat into annihilation.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The religious accounts differ. Lactantius has a dream and a sign painted on shields; Eusebius, writing after Constantine's death, adds a daytime vision and the labarum standard, which he says Constantine confirmed on oath. Some scholars doubt the vision, and the nature and timing of Constantine's conversion are debated. The bridge arrangements differ between accounts, and Eusebius frames the drowning as a re-enactment of Pharaoh's fate.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The narratives read here are Lactantius's On the Deaths of the Persecutors and Eusebius's Life of Constantine, both Christian works; Britannica's article, read in a browser, compares them. The Latin panegyrics were not read.

sources.title: Jordanes, The Origin and Deeds of the Goths (trans. Charles C. Mierow)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Displaced by the Huns, Gothic groups moved toward the Roman frontier. The Tervingi were admitted into the empire in 376, and the Greuthungi crossed without permission. Relations with Roman officials broke down and the Goths revolted. Jordanes, a Christian Goth who wrote in 551, probably in Constantinople, tells the Goths' side: they asked Valens for land in Thrace or Moesia, promising to obey his laws and to become Christians, and he gladly settled them as a wall against other peoples, sending Arian preachers. When famine came, the Roman commanders Lupicinus and Maximus sold them food at extortionate prices, even the flesh of dogs, until parents sold their children; Lupicinus then invited Fritigern to a feast and had his companions killed, and Fritigern cut his way out and led the Goths to war.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Valens, emperor in the East, had been campaigning in Syria and returned to deal with the revolt. His nephew Gratian, emperor in the West, had just defeated the Lentienses and was marching east to join him.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Ammianus says Valens, envious of Gratian's success and urged on by courtiers, wanted a victory of his own before his nephew arrived. Fritigern sought land in Thrace for his people and, in Ammianus's account, negotiated partly to gain time for his cavalry to return.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Livius places the battle about 13 km north of Adrianople (modern Edirne), near the village of Büyükdöllük. The Goths' wagons formed a ring on rising ground. It was a hot August day, and the Goths set fires to dry the plain.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Valens led his elite eastern troops, including veterans. Fritigern commanded the Tervingi, with Greuthungi under Alatheus and Saphrax, Alans and others. Ammianus says the scouts reported a far smaller Gothic force than was actually nearby, because the cavalry was away. Army sizes are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Valens fortified a camp near the city and held a council at which Sebastianus urged an attack and Victor urged waiting for Gratian. Valens marched out, leaving his baggage and treasury at Adrianople, and reached the Gothic wagon circle around the eighth hour. The right-wing cavalry deployed first while the rest of the column was still coming up.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Negotiations were still under way, with Richomeres volunteering as a hostage, when archers and light troops under Bacurius and Cassio attacked too early and fell back. The Gothic cavalry under Alatheus and Saphrax then returned and struck. The Roman left advanced almost to the wagons but, unsupported, was overwhelmed; the infantry was pressed so close together that it could hardly fight, and the line broke in dust and confusion.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Valens's decision to attack without waiting for Gratian, on a faulty scouting report and after a long march in the heat, is the central choice. Fritigern's negotiations, in Ammianus's view, bought time for the Gothic cavalry.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The return of the Gothic cavalry against a Roman army only partly deployed decided the battle.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Valens was killed and his body was never found; Ammianus gives two versions of his death. Jordanes follows one of them: wounded, Valens fled to a farm near Adrianople, and the Goths, not knowing an emperor lay hidden there, set fire to it. Many senior officers fell, and Ammianus compares the disaster with Cannae.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: A large part of the eastern field army and many experienced officers were lost. Valens's successor Theodosius made peace with the Goths by 382; Livius says he had to grant land to the victors, while Britannica says the Romans first drove the Goths back to Thrace.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Faulty intelligence, impatience and a tired, thirsty army deployed piecemeal against an enemy whose full strength was not yet in view. Waiting for the army to concentrate might have changed the outcome.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Ammianus treated the battle as a turning point; Livius says many later writers followed him although the view is not necessarily correct, while Britannica presents it as a victory of horsemen over elite infantry and the start of serious Germanic inroads. Livius's pages give two dates for Valens's death, 9 and 2 August. The circumstances of his death are uncertain, and Ammianus's figures for Roman losses are not repeated. Jordanes, whom his translator's edition calls a eulogist of the Gothic race, gives a Gothic and Catholic reading: he blames Roman greed and treachery for the revolt, says the Goths preferred to die fighting rather than of hunger, and calls Valens's burning the judgement of God on the emperor who had made the Goths Arians. His account of the battle itself is a single sentence.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.12–13 is the main narrative. Livius and Britannica, read in a browser, give modern summaries. Jordanes's Getica, in Charles Mierow's translation on Project Gutenberg, gives the only surviving account written from the Gothic side. Orosius was not read.

sources.title: Jordanes: The Battle of Châlons, 451 CE (Getica 38)
The battle of the Catalaunian Plains

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The Huns under Attila raided the Balkans from 440. In 447 Attila invaded the eastern empire's Balkan provinces, and Theodosius II raised his payments to him. Attila then turned west.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: In 451 the Huns crossed the Rhine, invaded Gaul and sacked Metz. Aetius, the leading Western Roman general, formed a coalition with the Visigothic king Theodoric and other peoples settled in Gaul.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Attila sought plunder and power in Gaul. Aetius needed to protect Gaul without breaking a coalition whose members had their own interests.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The site is unknown. The battle is variously called the Catalaunian Fields, the Campus Mauriacus or Châlons, and scholars place it north, east or west of Troyes. Jordanes describes a plain rising by a sharp slope to a ridge that both armies tried to take.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Aetius's coalition included Romans, Visigoths, Alans, Franks, Burgundians, Saxons and others. Attila's army included Ostrogoths, Gepids and other subject peoples under their own kings. Jordanes's figures for Attila's army and for the dead are not credible and are not repeated.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Jordanes places Theodoric and the Visigoths on the right, Aetius and the Romans on the left, and Attila with his best troops in the centre, with the subject peoples on the wings.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Attila was besieging Orléans when the coalition approached, and he withdrew, probably toward Troyes. In the battle both sides raced for the ridge; Thorismund, Theodoric's son, and Aetius reached it first and threw back the Huns. Dahm describes fighting from mid-afternoon into the night. Theodoric was killed, and the Visigoths pressed on almost to Attila, who withdrew into his wagon laager. Fighting in the dark was confused.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Taking the ridge first was the coalition's decisive tactical choice. Afterwards the allies chose to besiege Attila's laager rather than storm it, and, Jordanes says, quarrels between Romans and Goths let Attila escape.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The loss of the ridge and the Visigothic advance after Theodoric's death forced Attila onto the defensive behind his wagons.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Next morning the Huns stayed in their laager. Jordanes says Attila had a pyre of saddles built, meaning to throw himself on it rather than be captured. Attila then withdrew from Gaul.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Attila invaded Italy in 452, sacking Aquileia and other northern cities before returning home; Livius's timeline says Pope Leo persuaded him to go. Attila died in 453, and Aetius was assassinated in 454.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Coalition armies can win battles but struggle to finish them: once the immediate danger had passed, the allies' separate interests limited the pursuit. Dahm notes that the fighting was mainly a cavalry struggle for a ridge, not a clash on an open plain.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Jordanes wrote about a century later from a Gothic perspective; he drew on the eyewitness Priscus but goes beyond him, and his account, the fullest that survives, differs from others. The location and exact date are uncertain; Dahm gives 20 June. Dahm questions the traditional view of the battle as one of the most decisive in Western history, since Attila remained a threat. Why Aetius let Attila withdraw is not resolved by the sources read here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Jordanes's Getica 38, in an older translation on the Internet Medieval Sourcebook, is the main narrative. Murray Dahm's article for Osprey Publishing summarizes the modern debates, and Livius's articles supply the wider chronology. Hydatius's chronicle and the rest of the Getica were not read.
